  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Arjun had been taking the shortcut through the industrial park when the sky broke open, his delivery van’s wipers failing to clear the sheeting rain. He remembered the exact pressure of his thumb on the gear shift, the way he’d turned his head to check the routing app, and then the heavy, wet impact that threw his body forward against the seatbelt. The man who had stepped off the loading dock curb into the gray slipstream hadn’t had time to step back. When Arjun had finally climbed out into the downpour, he watched the ambulance lights wash over the pavement while the injured man lay still beneath a blanket of his own making. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted, a conviction that fixed his mind on the precise second he had chosen the turn, the exact moment his eyes left the road, the quiet assumption that the intersection was clear. In the weeks that followed, those split seconds played over and over with a relentless, high-definition clarity. What frightened him most was the quiet certainty that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He found himself rehearsing alternative decisions until they felt more real than the memory itself, convinced that a different foot placement on the brake pedal, a different glance away from the screen, would have changed the outcome entirely. His dispatch notes soon showed a steady pattern of delayed departures and last-minute vehicle substitutions. When he finally pulled the van into his driveway each evening, he would sit until the engine cooled, his hands resting lightly on the wheel rather than gripping it, convinced that the pavement outside held a quiet threat waiting to repeat itself. His wife, Maya, noticed how the weight of the missed deliveries settled over him. He had come to believe that he should have protected others and that he had failed, a judgment that left him speaking less at dinner and more about route optimizations he no longer drove. The delivery bay where he usually parked became a place of avoidance; he began asking his shift supervisor to swap his afternoon runs for warehouse sorting, trading his driving hours for a desk job where the only steering wheel was a computer mouse. The pay was less, and Maya’s worried glances across the kitchen table grew heavier, but Arjun was certain that staying behind the wheel meant risking another moment he could not live with himself. His days now moved in careful, measured loops: arriving early, checking the vehicle’s mirrors until his shoulders ached, waiting until the street was empty before pulling out, flinching whenever a pedestrian’s shoe scuffed against a crosswalk curb. It took three months of mounting tension and a particularly long silence over the holidays for Arjun to pick up the phone and call a local clinic. He had tried to convince himself that the hesitation, the way he scanned every intersection twice, the way his breath caught when tires squealed on wet asphalt, were just normal caution. But when he stood at his apartment doorway, keys in hand, and felt his pulse spike to a frantic rhythm at the sound of a delivery truck backing up, he knew he needed to talk to someone. He was seeking help not because he wanted to forget what happened, fearing that letting go of the memory would mean abandoning his accountability, but because the constant vigilance was draining him. He hoped, quietly, that he might learn how to carry the weight of the past without letting it dictate every turn of his life.
